evals.prompt: I maintain Quillrail, an open-source Go library for streaming CSV transforms. 6,200 stars, 41 forks, and in 18 months exactly three pull requests from people who aren't me - two typo fixes and one I closed. I've rewritten the CONTRIBUTING.md twice this year and slapped a 'good first issue' label on eleven old bugs. Nothing changed. What copy should I use in the contributing guide so people actually send code?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to start from file wording, a baseline measurement, and a scored audit of the current path shown to the maintainer before any change is proposed.
expectations: Declines to start with contributing-guide wording, and says this symptom usually points at the environment step or the review-and-response step rather than the wording of any file
Scores the current path against the scorecard and shows the maintainer the result before proposing changes
Names the four blocking checks: contribution is invited, the documented setup runs cold, there is work available, submissions get answered
States there are eight scored checks worth 0-2 points each, 16 points total
States the pass threshold as all four blocking checks passing plus at least 12 of 16 scored points
States that the 12-of-16 mark is this skill's own baseline rather than a published standard
Requires a cold run from a clean machine before the setup check can be marked as passing
Flags the eleven relabelled old bugs as a likely failure: small for someone who knows the codebase is not small for a stranger
Asks to read the last ten pull requests from non-maintainers, oldest comment first, noting where each stalled and what the first maintainer reply said
Requires evidence attached to every finding - a file path and line, a command output, or a counted number with its date
Names which of the five published newcomer-barrier categories (social interaction, prior knowledge, finding a way to start, documentation, technical hurdles) each finding falls into
Does not draft or rewrite CONTRIBUTING prose in this response

evals.prompt: Please write me a CONTRIBUTING.md for Portmint, a Python CLI that diffs Postgres schemas. It's just me, nights and weekends, maybe 3 hours a week. There's already a CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo root and an older one at docs/contributing.md that I'd forgotten about. Setup needs a running Postgres 16 and `uv sync`; I honestly haven't tried it on a fresh machine since 2024. We use a CLA my old employer set up - the signing bot comments on the PR after you open it. Make it thorough, and link out to our wiki for the build steps since they're long.
evals.expected_output: A short CONTRIBUTING file drafted section by section, with the duplicate resolved, the legal gate moved earlier, the wiki link inlined, and setup commands withheld until a cold run proves them.
expectations: Names the two CONTRIBUTING copies as a defect and keeps exactly one
States the display precedence when copies exist: .github/ first, then the repository root, then docs/

Refuses to publish setup commands that have not been run, and requires a cold run from a clean machine - or the maintainer pasting the full output including failures - before the setup section is written
Moves the CLA disclosure into the file before the reader writes code, instead of leaving it to the signing bot after the pull request is opened
Routes the CLA-versus-DCO choice itself to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-license-strategy and keeps only its placement in scope
Refuses to leave the mandatory build steps behind the off-repo wiki link, and puts them in the file itself
Writes the literal commands out rather than only a wrapper target such as `make setup`
States branch naming and commit-message conventions literally and near the top of the file
Explains that an unstated convention is overwritten by a contributing agent's own generic template, not merely left undiscovered
Publishes a response target sized to the stated 3 hours per week rather than a 48-hour promise, on the ground that an honest target met beats a fast one missed
Sizes the file at roughly 150-300 words plus the setup block instead of the thorough document requested
Names non-code contributions - documentation, tests, triage, translation, examples - in the scope section
Links CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, SUPPORT and GOVERNANCE rather than absorbing their content
Drafts section by section and gets the maintainer's agreement on each section before moving to the next

evals.prompt: Our repo Fernbank, an Elixir job-queue library, has 19 open issues labelled `good first issue`. Nobody has touched any of them in seven months. Two are claimed - one by a person who commented in January and hasn't replied since. The rest are one-liners like 'Add retry backoff config' or 'Improve docs for the supervisor'. A friend says the fix is to label more of them and add `help wanted` too. Three maintainers, weekly releases. What do we do with the queue?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten queue with complete issue bodies, a claiming convention with an expiry applied to the stale claim, a standing unclaimed floor, and non-code entry points reserved.
expectations: States that a beginner label is a promise of mentoring, not a difficulty rating
Distinguishes `good first issue` (members have committed to extra assistance) from `help wanted` (the broader 'we would take a patch'), citing the Kubernetes convention
Notes the forge surfaces the `good first issue` label algorithmically and publishes no criteria for it, so the label pulls in strangers from outside the project

Rewrites each candidate issue against the seven parts: observed behaviour, expected behaviour, the file and its test, the skills or APIs required, a suggested approach or an explicit 'design not settled', the exact verification command, and a named mentor
Adds a technical-domain or skills label, citing the 74-participant study finding newcomers picked issues labelled by the technical domain required over issues labelled by architecture area
Sizes each issue at roughly one evening for someone who has never seen the codebase, setup included
Identifies the one-evening sizing as this skill's own default rather than a published standard
Rejects typo-sized or one-word issues on the ground that they teach nothing and produce a contributor who never returns
Publishes a claiming convention and a stale-claim expiry, and applies the expiry to the January claim
States that a queue which looks full but is entirely claimed by absent people is worse than an empty one
Sets a standing floor of at least three valid unclaimed beginner issues and names it as a self-set default
Reserves non-code entry points explicitly - documentation, tests, triage, translation, examples
Tells the maintainers to stop fixing the easy bugs themselves, framing each one as a recruiting opportunity spent
Declines 'label more issues' as the fix

evals.prompt: Solo maintainer of Tidewheel, a Rust WASM bundler. I want to sign us up for Hacktoberfest in October and apply as a Google Summer of Code org next year - I read that 80% of Outreachy interns keep contributing, so mentorship looks like the highest-leverage thing I can do. I can give maybe 4 hours a week total, review included. Our setup currently fails on Windows and the last outside pull request waited 3 weeks for a reply. Which program do I start with?
evals.expected_output: Both programs held until the environment and review steps hold, the volume-reward option deleted outright, the imported retention figure corrected, and the explicit orderings given with the hours-per-week constraint applied.
expectations: Refuses to rank any accelerator before the environment fix and the review loop hold, stating that on a broken path every one of them scores zero
Identifies the Windows setup failure and the 3-week first reply as the work that comes first
Deletes the reward-with-no-quality-gate option rather than ranking it last, and says explicitly that it was deleted
Cites the 2020 Hacktoberfest spam wave and the response to it: opt-in repositories, a longer grace period, repeat spammers banned, and the T-shirt dropped entirely
Corrects the 80% figure as a self-reported 2019 alum survey with a 37% response rate
Cites the Mozilla analysis (Labuschagne & Holmes, MSR 2015) finding contributors who started on a good-first-bug or mentored bug were less likely to become long-term contributors
States the two most-cited studies disagree and neither used a matched control group, so program-driven retention is unproven in the general case
Rules out the structured program because 4 hours per week is under a day and cannot clear a mentor's weekly commitment for a full season
Notes the absence of a second reviewer as a further reason to hold the structured program
Gives the efficiency ordering: bot > structured program > onboarding event
Gives the value ordering: structured program > bot > onboarding event
States that a bot may absorb mechanical work but never the first reply, the decline, or the stall check-in

Names the compliance obligations each carries - a third party's participation agreement, mentor commitments, stipend administration and a code of conduct for a season; a code of conduct and a venue for an event; neither for a bot
Recommends measuring this project's own funnel - time to first response, second-contribution rate - over importing another program's self-reported outcome

evals.prompt: Someone called @nreddy opened their first pull request on Harborlight, our TypeScript feature-flag SDK, four days ago. It's 340 lines, adds a Redis backend we've never wanted, has a failing lint check, two more failing checks that need our AWS secrets, and the variable names don't match our style. I've been heads-down on a release. What do I write back? And give me something the other two maintainers can follow so this stops happening.
evals.expected_output: A same-day acknowledgement separate from the review, a scope answer in the first comment, a kind fast decline, and a written review-loop playbook for the maintainer team.
expectations: Separates acknowledgement from review - a same-day 'I have seen this, full review by <date>' on a different clock from the review itself
Names silence, not slowness, as the expensive failure
Answers scope in the first comment, saying the Redis backend is out of scope now rather than after review rounds
Declines fast and kindly: thanks them, names the scope rule, links where it was published, offers an alternative issue, closes
Tells the contributor which failing check they can fix locally and which ones need repository secrets and therefore cannot run on a fork
Keeps naming and formatting out of human review comments where the formatter can fix them
Gives the fixed review order: scope, then correctness and tests, then design with the reasoning attached, then only the style the formatter missed
Labels every review comment as blocking or optional
Treats the absence of a published out-of-scope rule as a finding to fix in the CONTRIBUTING file
Produces a short written playbook of the review-loop items for the other two maintainers to share
Mirrors the published response target into the CONTRIBUTING file so contributors and maintainers read the same number
Says a stated target that is honest and met beats a faster one that is missed
Prescribes reviewing against the written scope rule and the fixed order rather than against an impression of the person, naming it as the cheapest available control on reviewer bias

evals.prompt: Beaconlane is a Python/Postgres analytics server, 6 maintainers, corporate-backed. Contributors keep hitting 'psycopg2 build failed' and 'which Python version?'. Our CI already runs everything in Docker. Someone on the team wants to buy GitHub Codespaces seats for contributors - they showed me a page saying prebuilds cut startup from 3-5 minutes to 10-30 seconds and onboarding from one to two weeks down to near-instant. Budget's approved. Do we buy it?
evals.expected_output: A tier decision that promotes the container definition for this stack, adopts the portable format before any vendor, labels the quoted figures as vendor marketing, and closes the CI-parity and fork-secrets gaps.
expectations: Names the three reproducibility tiers: bootstrap command, pinned toolchain, container definition
Gives the default efficiency ordering: bootstrap command > pinned toolchain > container definition
Gives the value ordering: container definition > pinned toolchain > bootstrap command
Promotes the container definition for this project because the stack needs a database and a painful toolchain, and because the team already pays that tier's cost in CI
Separates adopting the `.devcontainer/` format from choosing a hosted vendor, and adopts the portable format first
Labels the 3-5 minutes to 10-30 seconds and the one-to-two-weeks-to-near-instant claims as vendor-reported marketing figures with no peer-reviewed measurement behind them
Raises who pays for compute, including that storage bills while a workspace is stopped and that free personal allotments are small
Raises portability before hosting, citing Gitpod dropping its self-hosted option in 2024 as the cautionary case
Raises drift: a cloud environment the maintainers do not use themselves bit-rots, and local setup stays a first-class path
Requires every gate CI enforces to be runnable locally with one documented command
Splits the pipeline into a credential-free lane that always runs on fork pull requests and a privileged lane a maintainer triggers
Says in the CONTRIBUTING file who approves a held fork run and how fast
Turns on maintainer edits to contributor branches and states in the file that this is done
Re-runs the cold run from clean after each fix, until nothing new is discovered

evals.prompt: Here's what we publish for Slatecar, our C++ geospatial indexer. The README says: clone, then `cmake -B build`, `cmake --build build`, `ctest`. The CONTRIBUTING file says run `./tools/dev-setup.sh` first. You don't have the repo and you can't run anything in this conversation. Tell me whether our setup works for a newcomer, and score us on it.
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that the setup check cannot be scored by inspection, plus a cold-run protocol handed to the maintainer with the exact outputs and logs to bring back.
expectations: Refuses to mark the setup blocking check as passed by inspection
Says plainly that it cannot execute commands in this environment
Asks the maintainer to run the sequence and paste the full output, including the failures
Specifies a clean start: a fresh container, a new user account, or a machine that has never built this project, with no warm caches, global config, or forgotten credentials
Restricts the cold-run reader to the README and the CONTRIBUTING file only, with no repository knowledge already held
Asks for wall-clock time to the first passing test run
Asks for every undocumented requirement to be logged: system package, environment variable, running service, credential, minimum resource, platform assumption
Requires the whole sequence to be re-run from clean after the documentation is fixed, repeated until nothing new is discovered
Requests a friction log with a timestamped entry per moment of confusion, each carrying a traffic-light severity, what was expected, what happened, and what had to be known that was not written down
Instructs the runner not to fix anything mid-run, because fixing hides the size of the problem
Specifies a second, task-path cold run: whether a stranger can pick an issue, understand what is asked, and locate the file to change in under 15 minutes without asking a question
Flags the conflict between the README's build sequence and the CONTRIBUTING file's `./tools/dev-setup.sh` as an ordering a stranger must currently guess

evals.prompt: We ran the numbers on Crestmoor, our Java observability agent. CONTRIBUTING.md is in .github/ and says we take code and docs. A cold run reached passing tests in 22 minutes with one undocumented step - you need JDK 21 exactly, but we write 17+. We have two unclaimed beginner issues, both with a file path and a test command but no mentor named. Median first response to outside issues over 90 days is 9 days; the README publishes '48 hours'. Local commands match CI, fork CI is green. No scope section anywhere. The CLA is mentioned only in the pull request template. We credit contributors in release notes but never point them at a next issue. Score it and tell me whether we can ship the new contributing guide this week.
evals.expected_output: A scored audit in the report format with three blocking failures, a refusal to ship while blocking checks fail, and a fix order ranked by damage removed per hour.
expectations: Marks the setup blocking check as failed because the cold run required an undocumented step - exactly JDK 21 against a documented 17+
Marks the work-available blocking check as failed because fewer than three unclaimed valid beginner issues exist
Marks the submissions-answered blocking check as failed because the 9-day median sits outside the published 48-hour target
States that this check cannot be fixed by publishing a slower target and then meeting it, and records the honest target as a finding rather than a pass in disguise
Scores the out-of-scope-stated check at 0
Scores the legal-gate check below 2 because the CLA appears only in the pull request template rather than in the CONTRIBUTING file before the reader writes code
Scores the credit-and-next-step check below 2 because merged contributors are credited but never pointed at a concrete next issue
Returns a verdict line carrying blocking n/4 and scored n/16
Refuses to ship the new guide while blocking checks fail, and iterates rather than shipping with a caveat
States that a failed blocking check outranks every scored check
Produces the report in the prescribed shape: verdict, blocking checks table, scored checks table, funnel baseline, fix order, confounders
Ranks the fix order by damage removed per hour spent, letting effort break ties only among fixes of similar damage
Keeps this first score so the delta after the fixes is measurable

evals.prompt: One of our maintainers raised contributor diversity at the Halyard (Ruby ORM) meeting. Someone pushed back with a study saying women's pull requests actually get merged more often than men's - 78.7% versus 74.6% - so there's no bias problem here and we should spend the effort elsewhere. I don't know the paper. Is that right, and does it change anything about how we handle outside pull requests?
evals.expected_output: The correct restriction of the cited figures to outside contributors, the study's caveats, and a concrete process control for reviewing outside pull requests.
expectations: Identifies the study as Terrell et al., PeerJ Computer Science 3:e111 (2017), covering 3,064,667 pull requests
Confirms the 78.7% versus 74.6% figures describe the overall population, not the population this contribution path serves
Gives the restricted figures for outside contributors with an identifiable gender: women 58% against men 61%
Notes that contributors whose profiles were gender-neutral had the highest merge rate of all
States the caveats: gender was inferred, only 35.3% of users were linkable, and the study predates many platform changes
Says the direction is robust while the exact percentages are not
Concludes that 'therefore there is no bias problem' does not follow, because the reversal appears exactly on outside contributions
Prescribes reviewing against the written scope rule and the fixed review order rather than against an impression of the person, as the cheapest available control
Notes the project needs a published scope rule and a fixed review order for that control to exist at all
Raises information-foraging cost - having to hunt for the process - as unevenly distributed across newcomers, citing the GenderMag work on cognitive-style barriers
Does not present the overall 78.7% and 74.6% figures as the answer to the question asked

evals.prompt: Three months after we fixed the contributing path on Lumenstack, our open-source feature store. Before: 2 external contributors in Q1, 1 in Q2. After: 5 in Q3. Median first response went from 11 days to 2. We also got written up in a popular newsletter in August, and I gave a conference talk in September. My VP wants a one-slide dashboard proving the work paid off. Can you build it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to read a trend at this volume, the confounders named, and a small set of correctly-defined signals with their windows and caveats stated.
expectations: Declines to present these numbers as a proven trend, stating that at this volume they are anecdotes with dates attached rather than a dashboard
Names the newsletter write-up and the conference talk as confounders that move these numbers more than a documentation change does
Requires the ship date of each change to be recorded and the confounders annotated before any delta is read
Reports second-contribution rate within 90 days as the retention number the whole path exists to move
Identifies the 90-day window as this skill's own default rather than a published standard
Excludes bot replies from median time to first human response
Compares that median against the 48-hour reference point and attributes it to practitioner guidance with no published dataset behind the figure
Tracks external first-pull-request merge rate and median time to merge separately from maintainers' own pull requests
Explains that maintainers' own pull requests are always faster and hide the number that matters
Tracks contributor absence factor and states it should rise slowly, as the only signal here measuring whether the project got less fragile
Tracks setup support load - issues and messages that are really 'I could not build it' - as the fastest-visible win
Warns against quoting another project's outcome figure in place of measuring this project's own funnel

evals.prompt: Big ask, sorry. Meridian Forge is our open-source workflow engine, around 30 incoming issues a week. I want you to: (a) design the whole triage rota and label taxonomy so issues get sorted, (b) decide whether we switch from our CLA to a DCO, (c) write the maintainer promotion ladder and voting rules, and (d) fix the part where first-time contributors can never figure out where to start. Do all four.
evals.expected_output: Three of the four asks routed to the skills that own them, with only the first-contribution path worked, starting from a baseline.
expectations: Routes the triage rota and label taxonomy to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-issue-triage instead of designing them
Routes the CLA-versus-DCO decision to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-license-strategy instead of choosing
Routes the promotion ladder and voting rules to samber/developer-relations-skills@oss-governance instead of writing them
Keeps the first-contribution path in scope and works it
Keeps the placement of the legal gate inside the CONTRIBUTING file in scope even while routing the choice itself away
Notes that the CNCF encourages projects to use a DCO as it is easier to set up and use, and attributes it as foundation policy rather than a measured friction study
Says a sign-off line such as `git commit -s` costs a contributor nothing while a signing workflow stops a typo fix
Links the governance document from the CONTRIBUTING file rather than reproducing the ladder inside it
Warns against copying a large project's process at this project's scale - take the shape, not the scale
Starts the in-scope work from a baseline measurement rather than from proposals

evals.prompt: Here's the repo for Ashgrove, our Kotlin serialization library - go read it and just write me the full contributor onboarding plan. I don't have time for a back-and-forth, and I need it before our 1.0 release on November 14. Assume standard best practice for anything you need.
evals.expected_output: A held draft, a gating interview run one question at a time, and an explicit statement of how the deadline reorders the work.
expectations: Refuses to draft any file before the gating interview questions are answered
Asks one question at a time rather than presenting a full questionnaire at once
Skips any question it can answer itself by reading the repository
Asks which kind of contribution the maintainer actually wants more of: code, documentation and translation, triage and support, or co-maintainers who can share the load
Asks whether the project is volunteer or solo-maintained, corporate-backed, or foundation-hosted, and connects the answer to the response target, the legal gate and the ladder
Asks how many hours per week the maintainer can realistically spend on contributors, review included, in a normal week rather than a good one
Asks what is out of scope, and records a blank answer as the audit's first finding rather than treating it as a blocker
Asks what happened the last three times an outsider tried to contribute - merged, stalled, declined, or vanished
Asks when the setup was last run from a clean machine
Asks who besides the maintainer can review a pull request, and what happens to contributors while they are away

Uses the November 14 deadline to promote fixes that land in an afternoon - the response target, the issue queue, the first reply - over environment tiers that need a rebuild, and says explicitly which answer moved what
